statusDescriptions.discussed: Discussed by the City or at a Council meeting
statusDescriptions.benchmark: Not proposed in Hollister; a tool other California cities use

actions.name: Interfund loan from impact fee funds
actions.amountBasis: The City's own October 2026 infographic states $11M borrowing "to support cash flow and prior deficits."
actions.desc: The City borrowed $11M into the General Fund to support cash flow and prior deficits.
actions.consequence: Near-term operating cash, not a reduction in ongoing spending. It is repayable by June 30, 2027, and the structural gap is exactly as large after it as before.
actions.realNote: Approved October 2, 2026, the night the Council declared a financial emergency.
actions.rateNote: City staff have been quoted putting the rate at 4%; the adopted resolution has been described as stating 3-4%. The resolution text is not published on the City website, so both are recorded.

sources.title: A Clear Look At Our Financial Situation

actions.name: Hotel tax increase (Measure V)
actions.amountBasis: Already enacted, so it adds nothing further. The City's ballot language estimated approximately $300,000.00 annually.
actions.desc: Voters raised the transient occupancy tax from 8% to 12%, effective April 1, 2025.
actions.consequence: Already enacted and already inside the $975,000 of hotel tax in the adopted budget. Nothing further to claim.
actions.realNote: Ballot question: a four percentage point (4%) increase "increasing the total tax levied on hotel occupants from 8 to 12 percent … generating approximately $300,000.00 annually."

actions.name: Updated building permit and user fees
actions.amountBasis: Already in effect before the adopted budget, so it adds nothing further to it.
actions.desc: The City published an updated building permit and user fee schedule on July 23, 2026.
actions.consequence: Already in effect, so its yield is already inside the $4,211,000 of licences and permits in the adopted budget.

sources.title: Updated Building Permit and User Fees

actions.name: Layoff notices
actions.desc: On October 14, 2026 the City began issuing layoff notices to represented and unrepresented employees across multiple departments.
actions.consequence: The City published neither a headcount nor a savings amount. Animal Control staff are unaffected and the City says it is not eliminating all civilian positions.
actions.realNote: Announced October 14, 2026 with no number of positions and no dollar figure.

sources.title: Press release: workforce reductions and financial emergency
Press release #2: workforce reductions and financial emergency

actions.name: Voluntary separation and retirement incentives
actions.desc: The City offered voluntary separation and retirement incentives in July 2026. Several employees accepted.
actions.consequence: The City states these did not generate sufficient savings. No savings figure has been published.
actions.realNote: October 14, 2026: "voluntary workforce reductions did not generate sufficient savings."

sources.title: Press release #2: workforce reductions and financial emergency

actions.name: Cancelled contracts with non-profits
actions.desc: The City reports it has cancelled historical contracts with non-profit organisations.
actions.consequence: Named by the City among the conditions that led to the emergency declaration. No dollar value published.

actions.name: Release the budgeted contingency
actions.amountBasis: Account 101-1100-999999 CONTINGENCY in the adopted budget: $1,200,000.
actions.desc: Spend down the contingency the adopted budget sets aside in the non-departmental account.
actions.consequence: One-time by definition, and it is the cushion for the next unbudgeted failure.

actions.name: Work reductions: 5% of payroll
actions.amountBasis: 5% of the adopted budget's published General Fund personnel total of $34,954,900. The 5% depth is this game's illustration, not a City figure.
actions.desc: The City states work reductions will take place and that payroll is its largest cost.
actions.consequence: Could be delivered as layoffs, furloughs or attrition. The depth is a choice; the City has not published one.

sources.title: Press release #2: workforce reductions and financial emergency

actions.name: Cancel the events budget
actions.amountBasis: EVENT EXPENDITURES, account centre 1140 in the adopted budget: $500,000.
actions.desc: The City lists community programs among the services that could be reduced.
actions.consequence: Hollister without its events calendar saves real money and costs the downtown businesses that depend on those weekends.

actions.name: Cut services and supplies by 10%
actions.amountBasis: 10% of the published General Fund services and supplies total of $9,700,350. The 10% depth is this game's illustration.
actions.desc: The City lists administrative services among the areas that could be reduced.
actions.consequence: Spread thinly across every department. It is the easiest cut to make and the easiest to reverse.

actions.name: Cut contracted services by 5%
actions.amountBasis: 5% of the published General Fund contractual total of $11,896,300. The 5% depth is this game's illustration.
actions.desc: Reviewing contracts is one of the steps named in the City's financial emergency response.
actions.consequence: Much of this is dispatch, legal and solid waste under contract. Some of it cannot be cut without renegotiating.

actions.name: Defer capital outlay
actions.amountBasis: The published General Fund capital total in the adopted budget: $297,900.
actions.desc: Deferring equipment and capital purchases is among the cost reductions the City describes.
actions.consequence: Pushes cost into later years rather than removing it.

actions.name: Reduce hours and service levels
actions.desc: The City says residents can expect shorter hours, fewer days of operation, longer wait times, and reduced maintenance, recreation, permitting and community programs.
actions.consequence: Already beginning: on October 14, 2026 the police lobby was open 8-10 a.m. and records and general customer service were limited. No figure published.

sources.title: Press release: workforce reductions and financial emergency

actions.name: Shift customer service to AI
actions.desc: The City lists more AI customer service among the changes residents can expect.
actions.consequence: Named by the City as an expected change. No figure published.

actions.name: Sell assets
actions.desc: Selling assets is one of the steps named in the City's financial emergency proclamation.
actions.consequence: One-time money by definition. No specific asset or amount has been published.

actions.name: Collect outstanding debt
actions.desc: Collecting debt owed to the City is one of the steps named in the financial emergency proclamation.
actions.consequence: Money the City is already owed rather than new revenue. No total published.

actions.name: Additional 1% sales tax
actions.amountBasis: No tax is enacted, so current revenue from this proposal is $0.
actions.desc: In October 2026 the Council authorised staff to pursue special state legislation that would let the City raise its sales tax cap by up to 1%.
actions.consequence: This did not impose a tax, set a rate, or place a measure on the ballot. Legislation, a later Council action and voter approval would all be required first.

scenario.label: If a full additional 1% were enacted
scenario.basis: Inferred by matching the existing 1% Measure W transactions-and-use tax, which the adopted budget projects at $9,682,000. An inference from the existing tax, not an official forecast for a new one.

actions.realNote: The October 2, 2026 action only authorised pursuing special state legislation.

actions.name: Full cost-recovery fee study
actions.amountBasis: 5% of the adopted budget's published charges for services ($10,753,700). A benchmark for this game, not a Hollister proposal or estimate.
actions.desc: Reset permit, plan-check and service fees to the true cost of providing them. Routine practice in California cities closing a gap.
actions.consequence: Council can set these without a vote. The development community will fight it, and it takes a study to defend.

actions.name: Modernise the business licence tax
actions.amountBasis: Doubling the adopted budget's published business licence line ($240,000). A benchmark for this game, not a Hollister proposal or estimate.
actions.desc: Move a flat-rate business licence schedule to gross receipts. Widely used by California cities whose schedules have not changed in decades.
actions.consequence: Overdue housekeeping in most cities that do it. Small businesses still feel it as a rate increase.

actions.name: Raise the hotel tax two more points
actions.amountBasis: The adopted budget's published hotel tax ($975,000) divided by the current 12% rate, times two points. A benchmark for this game, not a Hollister proposal or estimate.
actions.desc: Take the transient occupancy tax from 12% to 14%. Several California cities sit at 14% or above.
actions.consequence: Visitors pay it, not residents, which is why it is usually the easiest tax measure to pass. It still needs voter approval.

actions.name: Increase the property transfer tax
actions.amountBasis: Doubling the adopted budget's published property transfer tax line ($225,000). A benchmark for this game, not a Hollister proposal or estimate.
actions.desc: Raise the tax charged when property changes hands. A common charter-city revenue tool in California.
actions.consequence: Revenue rises and falls with the housing market, so it is among the least predictable sources a city can lean on.

actions.name: Review franchise fee agreements
actions.amountBasis: 10% of the adopted budget's published franchise fee total ($1,177,000). A benchmark for this game, not a Hollister proposal or estimate.
actions.desc: Renegotiate the fees utilities and haulers pay to use the public right of way. Routine when agreements come up for renewal.
actions.consequence: Utilities generally pass the increase through to the same residents on their monthly bills.
